questions.prompt: Sonia joined the neighbourhood aid group when she was fifteen, and she is still a member of it today. Which sentence says so?

options.text: Sonia is a member of the group since she was fifteen.
Sonia was a member of the group since she was fifteen.
Sonia has been a member of the group since she was fifteen.
Sonia has been a member of the group since almost three years.

questions.explanation: The period starts at a point in the past and runs right up to today, so the main verb is a present perfect and since gives the point where it begins: "Sonia has been a member of the group since she was fifteen." "Sonia is a member of the group since she was fifteen." puts a plain present after since, which cuts the sentence off from the fifteen-year-old she was. "Sonia was a member of the group since she was fifteen." shuts the whole period inside the past, so she would have left the group by now. "Sonia has been a member of the group since almost three years." keeps the right tense but replaces the starting point with a length of time, and a length takes for, never since.

questions.prompt: Complete: "My aunt gives blood four times a year, and the hospital has known her as a regular ___ since 2011."

options.text: donating
donation
donator
donor

questions.explanation: The gap follows an article and an adjective and names a person, and the person built on donate is "donor", with -or on a shortened stem. "donation" names the act of giving, not the one who gives. "donator" adds -or to the whole verb, which English refuses here even though it accepts actor and visitor. "donating" is the -ing form of the verb and can never follow a regular.

questions.prompt: Read: "When their mother could no longer manage the family bakery, Nadia stopped studying and ran it herself." Which sentence reports what Nadia did?

options.text: She caught up with her studies and stayed up in the bakery.
She gave up the bakery and took over her studies.
She grew up her studies and cared for the bakery.
She took over the bakery and gave up her studies.

questions.explanation: take over means to assume responsibility for something and give up means to abandon, which is exactly what running the bakery and stopping her studies amount to: "She took over the bakery and gave up her studies." "She gave up the bakery and took over her studies." swaps the two verbs and says she abandoned the bakery, the opposite of running it. "She grew up her studies and cared for the bakery." uses grow up, which means to attain maturity and never takes an object. "She caught up with her studies and stayed up in the bakery." reads catch up with as going back to her courses and stay up as remaining awake, and the text reports neither.

questions.prompt: A visitor has just claimed that young people never give anything. The speaker answers with the emphatic form, to insist that the opposite is true. Which sentence is correctly built?

options.text: Our students do give every year.
Our students do gave every year.
Our students are giving every year.
Our students give every year.

questions.explanation: The emphatic form puts do, does or did in front of the base verb of an ordinary affirmative sentence, and that is what pushes the fact back at somebody who doubts it: "Our students do give every year." "Our students give every year." states the same fact with no insistence whatever, so it answers the visitor without contradicting her. "Our students do gave every year." leaves the past ending on the main verb although do has already taken the tense; only the base form can follow. "Our students are giving every year." puts a fact repeated every year into the continuous, which describes one moment in progress instead.

questions.prompt: The school collected winter clothes in a store room and planned to send them out in December. The boxes were still there in February. Which sentence says so?

options.text: The boxes should leave the store room in December.
The boxes should have left the store room in December.
The boxes should have leave the store room in December.
The boxes shouldn't have left the store room in December.

questions.explanation: should plus have plus a past participle names the sensible thing that did not happen, which is exactly the case of boxes still sitting there in February: "The boxes should have left the store room in December." "The boxes should leave the store room in December." gives advice about a December still to come, and this December is over. "The boxes shouldn't have left the store room in December." says they did leave and that leaving was a mistake, the opposite of the facts. "The boxes should have leave the store room in December." drops the past participle that this structure always needs: after have the form is left.
